events.text: Blue shells, returning tide. Inspired by the NPS California mussel record: three unequal shells on wet rock. I will join dark shell planes with long curves and keep one compact cool reflection. Color coverage and raised relief will be judged separately.
The first washes leave pale linen lanes. Four broad wet bridges will connect them before the rock and shells.
Wet bridges closed the linen lanes, while soft horizontal bands remain. I will make a low, warm-grey rock with four broad connected planes.
The rock reads as an arch with a pale hollow. Broad interior overlaps will close it; lighter top planes should stay narrower than its body.
The rock hollow is closed, with regular relief across its surface. The near shell will lean upward to the right; broad dark passes will establish its filled belly.
The near shell has a pale interior slit and a faceted shoulder. A wide interior sweep will close the slit; the second shell will lean left and remain smaller.
The near shell slit is closed; two unequal dark masses share a root. A low third shell will spread rightward, then its lighter plane can separate it from the near shell.
Three filled shells read at whole view, but their shared root is too uniform. Long slate-blue planes will turn each shell toward light without outlining every edge.
Slate planes separate the three forms, though they still look like raised ribbons. A few thin growth curves will cross the near shell, kept darker than its light plane.
Thin growth curves are visible without taking over the near shell. I will repeat them more sparsely on the small shells and use one dark overlap seam at the foot.
The seam separates the overlap but forms a hard dark smile. A broader near-shell plane should partly absorb it; low ochre-green weed will balance the left margin.
The wider seam cover changed little; the weed has a detached right blade. Crossing its base into the stem will join it. Two wider weed bellies will make blades rather than wire.
The weed blades now join, but their turns are angular. I will seat the shells with short attachment threads and add two small pale barnacle bodies to the rock.
The small barnacles stay quiet; thread lines are barely visible. One short cool reflection on the near shoulder will be inspected alone before any supporting lights.
The eight-pixel reflection is visible at both scales and remains short. Three supporting marks will shape its blue surround and give the barnacles small recessed mouths.
The reflection stayed compact, and the barnacle mouths read as tiny recesses. The water still has horizontal bands; oblique wet veils can interrupt them without adding oil relief.
The veils softened bands only slightly. Dense curved shoulder passes should round the shell tips while keeping their unequal sizes and the short reflection.
The shoulder passes modestly softened interior turns; the outside facets and root seam remain. Warm reflected planes along the lower edges can make the shells belong to the rock.

The warm edge marks became three conspicuous crescents. Broader blue planes will reduce their contrast while leaving small warm interruptions; this is a color correction, not a promise to flatten relief.
Loaded blue covers reduced all three warm crescents; raised patches remain and the root seam is shorter. I will add a broken water edge and a darker rock crack, avoiding a continuous outline.
The wet water edge is very quiet; the rock crack is subdued. More opaque short water gestures will test whether a broken foam accent can be visible without rivaling the shell reflection.
Opaque foam is visible as two short segments. The lower shell acquired another pale rim; I will broaden its body over that rim, then sharpen only the barnacle lips.
Lower review: foam stays broken and the barnacles remain subordinate. The broad lower-shell cover reduced its pale rim, but a raised seam survives.

Lower review shows broken foam and small barnacle lips; the rock still carries broad relief pads. Two subdued brown shell patches and two tapered weed tips can add material variation without enlarging the light.
Brown patches are more conspicuous than intended. I will reduce them with blue, then broaden the upper shell turns. The goal is a quieter material hint, not two new focal spots.

Blue covers quieted the brown spots, leaving patch relief. The upper silhouettes are a little rounder but still faceted. Long wet top passes will close the remaining linen border and soften the band behind the group.

Top linen is covered; soft water bands remain. The rock has blunt ends and a pale central pad. Short oblique stone planes should turn the ends and reduce that pad without tracing the entire shoreline.
Stone covers changed the ends but left textured patches. I will give the weed two quiet midribs, reconnect its foot, and deepen one short shell contact rather than draw another full rim.

Weed midribs are quiet and its foot is joined. The root seam is still a short dark hook. One wider near-shell belly and three matched surface planes will reduce abrupt transitions before the final light check.
The wider belly reduced seam contrast but kept a hook and raised patch. Final refinement: restore the short reflection, close one crown turn, connect a weed tip and keep the near barnacle lip small.

Finished at 112 marks. Three filled unequal shells hold one compact reflection; broad covers closed a pale slit and reduced bright crescents, while relief, a short root hook, faceted shoulders and banded water remain. I will stop before more covers enlarge the patches.

creation.goal: Join dark mussel shell planes with long curves and retain one compact cool reflection; assess color coverage separately from raised relief.
